passages.happening:
Abraham moves south into the Negev and stays for a while in Gerar (verse 1). There he says of his wife, “She is my sister.” So Abimelech king of Gerar had Sarah brought to him (verse 2).

One night God comes to Abimelech in a dream: “You are as good as dead because of the woman you have taken, for she is a married woman” (verse 3).

Abimelech has not touched her. He answers, “Lord, would You destroy a nation even though it is innocent?” (verse 4). Abraham said she was his sister, and she said he was her brother. “I have done this in the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands” (verse 5).

God agrees: “Yes, I know that you did this with a clear conscience, and so I have kept you from sinning against Me” (verse 6). Abimelech must give Sarah back, “for he is a prophet; he will pray for you and you will live” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The Negev is the dry country in the far south of Canaan. Gerar lay in its western part, between Gaza and Beersheba. Many archaeologists place it at a large mound called Tel Haror, though not all agree.

The first hearers would groan at this point. Abraham did exactly this in Egypt, years before (12:10-20). God rescued Sarah then. Now he does it again. And the timing is the worst it could be. In chapter 18 God promised that Sarah would have a son within a year. In chapter 21 the son is born. In between, Abraham hands the mother of the promised child to another man.

Abimelech's name means ‘my father is king’. It may have been a royal title, used by more than one ruler. This chapter does not say why he took Sarah. Unlike chapter 12, it says nothing about her beauty, and she is about ninety (17:17). Many readers think a marriage tie with a rich newcomer was the point: Abraham had large flocks and many servants.

God speaks to a foreign king in a dream, and the king answers him honestly. Abimelech uses the word ‘integrity’, which means a whole and honest heart. God does not argue. He says he himself kept Abimelech from sinning.

Then comes a surprise. God calls Abraham ‘a prophet’. This is the first time the word appears in the Bible. Here a prophet is someone who stands close to God and prays for others, not mainly someone who tells the future.
passages.later:
A psalm looks back on these years of wandering: “He rebuked kings on their behalf” (Psalm 105:14). God said, “Do not touch My anointed ones! Do no harm to My prophets!” (Psalm 105:15).

Later prophets are often people who pray for others. Samuel tells Israel, “far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you” (1 Samuel 12:23). The people ask Jeremiah to “pray to the LORD your God on behalf of this entire remnant” (Jeremiah 42:2).

Isaac will tell the same lie about his wife in the same town (Genesis 26:7). Fear runs in families.
passages.hard:
Why does Genesis tell such a similar story three times (chapters 12, 20 and 26)? Readers explain it in two main ways.

Many critical scholars think the three are versions of one old story, kept by different groups and placed side by side when Genesis was put together. Other scholars, including many who hold that Genesis is one work, answer that such things could well happen more than once to herders who lived among local kings, and that the writer places them on purpose to show a family failing in the same way again and again. On either view, the point is the same: the promise keeps being put at risk by the people who carry it, and God keeps it safe.
passages.asks: God called Abraham a prophet on the very day Abraham had failed. Ask whether you think God can use only people with a clean record. Then notice that he kept Abimelech from sin, and he kept Sarah safe, when the man of faith did neither.

passages.happening:
Early the next morning Abimelech tells his servants everything, and “the men were terrified” (verse 8).

He calls Abraham and asks, “What have you done to us? How have I sinned against you, that you have brought such tremendous guilt upon me and my kingdom? You have done things to me that should not be done” (verse 9). “What prompted you to do such a thing?” (verse 10).

Abraham answers, “I thought to myself, ‘Surely there is no fear of God in this place. They will kill me on account of my wife’” (verse 11). Besides, he says, she really is his half-sister, the daughter of his father but not of his mother (verse 12). Ever since he left home he has asked her to say, “He is my brother” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Notice who fears God in this story. Abraham thought there was ‘no fear of God’ in Gerar. To fear God, in the Bible, means to honor him so much that it shapes how you live. Yet when Abimelech tells his servants about the dream, they are terrified. The king asks the right questions. He speaks of guilt and of things ‘that should not be done’. The foreigner is the one with a working conscience.

A newcomer with no land and no family nearby was in real danger in that world. Abraham's fear was not foolish. A local lord could kill a man to take his wife. But he was wrong about these people, and wrong about what God would do.

Abraham's excuse has three parts: I was afraid, it was half true, and we have always done this. Sarah was his half-sister (verse 12). Marriage to a half-sister was known in the ancient world, though the later law of Moses forbids it. But a half-truth told to deceive is still a lie, as the note on Genesis 12 says.

And verse 13 reveals that the lie was a plan from the start, a habit carried from place to place. He calls it Sarah's ‘loyalty’ to him. The word is a strong one, used elsewhere of faithful love. Abraham has turned it into a cover for his fear.
passages.later:
Israel's law later forbids marriage to a half-sister: “You must not have sexual relations with your sister, either your father’s daughter or your mother’s daughter” (Leviticus 18:9). Abraham lived before that law was given.

The fear of God is the root of wisdom: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10). And Job, who lived in the land of Uz and is never said to be an Israelite, is described as “blameless and upright, fearing God and shunning evil” (Job 1:1). The Bible keeps finding the fear of God in people outside the chosen family.
passages.hard:
This is a story about a man of faith who was rebuked, rightly, by a man outside the faith.

Abraham does not apologize. He explains. He was afraid; it was partly true; he had always done it. The text lets his words stand, and they sound thin beside Abimelech's question. The outsider behaves better than the prophet.

That is uncomfortable, and it should be. God's people are not better than others by nature. Abraham had heard God's promises, and he still assumed the worst about strangers and put his wife at risk to protect himself. The Bible does not hide this. It tells it so that readers will not trust in Abraham, but in the God who kept his promise in spite of Abraham.
passages.asks: Abraham assumed that people who did not share his faith would have no conscience, and he was wrong. Ask whom you have written off in the same way. Then ask whether someone outside the faith has ever spoken more truly to you than you deserved.

passages.t: Sarah restored, and a prayer that heals
passages.happening:
Abimelech gives Abraham sheep and cattle and servants, and gives Sarah back to him (verse 14). He says, “Look, my land is before you. Settle wherever you please” (verse 15).

To Sarah he says, “See, I am giving your brother a thousand pieces of silver. It is your vindication before all who are with you; you are completely cleared” (verse 16).

“Then Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech and his wife and his maidservants, so that they could again bear children” (verse 17). The LORD had closed every womb in Abimelech's household “on account of Abraham’s wife Sarah” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The king does more than return Sarah. He gives gifts, and he opens his land to Abraham. He treats the man who wronged him with generosity.

The thousand pieces of silver are a public payment. The Hebrew calls it ‘a covering of the eyes’, a phrase whose exact sense is debated. Most take it to mean a payment that clears Sarah's name before everyone, so that no one can say she was disgraced. The king makes sure Sarah is honored. Some readers hear an edge in his words: he calls Abraham ‘your brother’, repeating the lie back to them.

In that world children were a household's future. A house where no one could bear children would have known that something was wrong between it and God.

Then Abraham prays, and God heals. The man who caused the trouble is the one God uses to end it. That is the strangest grace in the chapter.

The chapter ends with wombs opened. Abimelech's household could bear children again. In the very next chapter Sarah, who has never had a child, becomes pregnant. God opens wombs, and he is about to open hers.
passages.later:
God's healing through a flawed man's prayer looks ahead. James writes, “pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail” (James 5:16), and then points to Elijah, “a man just like us” (James 5:17).

The next chapter opens: “Now the LORD attended to Sarah as He had said” (Genesis 21:1).
passages.asks: Abraham, who had done the wrong, prayed for the man he had wronged, and God answered. Ask whether there is someone you have harmed whom you could pray for today. Then ask whether you need to do more than pray: to say plainly that you were wrong.
